insider_note: Every King's-property question in this chapter follows the same three moves: replace x by (the limit sum minus x), add the two forms so the x cancels, then solve the x-free integral that remains.

steps.label: Apply the King's property
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Get this line exactly right before adding — a sign slip here ruins everything after it.
steps.memory_tip: sin(π − x) = sinx (same sign), cos(π − x) = −cosx (sign flips, but squaring removes it).
steps.why: The King's property replaces x by π − x inside the same limits. Since sin(π − x) = sinx and cos(π − x) = −cosx (and cos² removes the sign), the denominator is unchanged while the x in the numerator turns into π − x — this is what lets I cancel with itself later.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that cos²(π − x) = cos²x, so wrongly changing the denominator.
Writing sin(π − x) as −sinx instead of +sinx.

steps.label: Add and reduce to an x-free integral
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. This is the whole point of the King's property — the x disappears.
steps.memory_tip: x + (π − x) always cancels to a plain π — that is the signal the property worked.
steps.why: Adding the two equal forms of I cancels the x term (x + (π − x) = π), leaving a single, x-free integral that is easy to solve by substitution.
common_mistakes: Adding the numerators but not combining them over the common denominator correctly.
Losing the factor of 1/2 when isolating I.

steps.label: Substitute cosx = t and integrate
steps.margin_note: Two marks for the substitution and its new limits.
steps.memory_tip: cosx = t always turns sinx dx into −dt — this pair is used again and again in this chapter.
lines: Put cosx = t ⇒ −sinx dx = dt, so sinx dx = −dt
x = 0 ⇒ t = cos0 = 1; x = π ⇒ t = cosπ = −1
steps.why: cosx = t turns sinx dx into a plain −dt, and 1 + cos²x becomes 1 + t² — a standard Tan⁻¹ form. Flipping the limits absorbs the negative sign.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to flip the limits when the negative sign is absorbed.
Writing the antiderivative as log(1 + t²) instead of Tan⁻¹t.

steps.label: Evaluate the limits
steps.memory_tip: Tan⁻¹(1) and Tan⁻¹(−1) are a pair: π/4 and −π/4 — their difference is always π/2.
steps.why: Tan⁻¹(1) = π/4 and Tan⁻¹(−1) = −π/4, so subtracting gives π/2 exactly — a clean angle pair that makes the final multiplication easy.
common_mistakes: Writing Tan⁻¹(−1) as +π/4 instead of −π/4, which would give the wrong final value.
Leaving the answer as (π/2)(π/2) instead of simplifying to π²/4.
